landmarks.name: Old Faithful
landmarks.info: The most predictable big geyser in the world, which is the whole of its fame: every sixty to a hundred and ten minutes, thirty to fifty-five metres of water for one and a half to five minutes. Its cone is geyserite laid down a grain at a time over centuries. Here it goes every two minutes, because nobody would wait ninety.

landmarks.name: Castle Geyser
landmarks.info: Its cone is the biggest in the basin and perhaps the oldest - thousands of years of sinter. Goes about every fourteen hours for twenty minutes, then roars with steam for half an hour more.

landmarks.name: Grand Geyser
landmarks.info: The tallest predictable geyser: a fountain rather than a column, in bursts, up to sixty metres, every six hours or so.

landmarks.name: Beehive Geyser
landmarks.info: A narrow cone like a nozzle, and a column to match: fifty metres, straight up, once or twice a day.

landmarks.name: Riverside Geyser
landmarks.info: Leans out over the Firehole in an arch, every six hours, for twenty minutes.

landmarks.name: Daisy Geyser
landmarks.info: Goes at an angle, a fan of water every couple of hours.

landmarks.name: Great Fountain Geyser
landmarks.info: Lower Geyser Basin's big one: a wide terraced sinter platform that floods, and then bursts of up to sixty metres over an hour.

landmarks.name: Steamboat Geyser
landmarks.info: The tallest active geyser in the world - over ninety metres - and the least predictable: years can go by between major eruptions, or days. It splashes in between. Here it goes rarely, and when it does it is enormous.

landmarks.name: Echinus Geyser
landmarks.info: An acid geyser - rare anywhere - in a pool rimmed with iron-red and black.

landmarks.name: Clepsydra Geyser
landmarks.info: Has hardly stopped erupting since the 1959 Hebgen Lake earthquake.

landmarks.name: Lone Star Geyser
landmarks.info: Out on its own up the Firehole, with a cone five metres tall. Every three hours.

landmarks.name: Grand Prismatic Spring
landmarks.info: The largest hot spring in the United States: a hundred and twelve metres across and fifty deep, blue in the middle where it is too hot for anything to live, and then green, yellow, orange and red outward where the bacterial mats grow at the temperature each can stand. The steam over it takes the colour on a still morning.

landmarks.name: Excelsior Geyser Crater
landmarks.info: A crater of a spring, a hundred metres by two hundred, that pours four thousand gallons a minute into the Firehole. It erupted three hundred feet in the 1880s and blew itself apart.

landmarks.name: Morning Glory Pool
landmarks.info: It used to be blue all the way down. A century of coins, rocks and rubbish thrown in has blocked the vent, the water has cooled, and the orange and yellow bacteria have moved in from the edge.

landmarks.name: Sapphire Pool
landmarks.info: Biscuit Basin's deep clear blue, named for the colour.

landmarks.name: Emerald Pool
landmarks.info: Green because yellow bacteria line a blue pool.

landmarks.name: Abyss Pool
landmarks.info: West Thumb: sixteen metres deep and you can see the bottom.

landmarks.name: Fishing Cone
landmarks.info: A cone standing in the lake itself. Anglers used to catch a trout off it and boil it on the hook without moving.

landmarks.name: Mammoth Hot Springs Terraces
landmarks.info: Travertine, not sinter: limestone dissolved underground and laid back down as the water cools and loses its gas, two tonnes a day. The terraces grow, go dry and white, and start somewhere else. Minerva is the famous one, and it switches on and off by the decade.

landmarks.name: Liberty Cap
landmarks.info: A hot-spring cone eleven metres tall, built up by one vent over perhaps two and a half thousand years, which then stopped.

landmarks.name: Mud Volcano
landmarks.info: Acid ground where there is too little water for a spring: the rock rots to clay and boils. Dragon's Mouth Spring roars in its cave mouth. The Mud Volcano itself blew its own cone off in the 1870s.

landmarks.name: Fountain Paint Pot
landmarks.info: Mud boiling in shades of cream and pink, with the colour from iron oxides; thick in late summer when it is dry, thin in spring.

landmarks.name: Lower Falls of the Yellowstone
landmarks.info: Ninety-four metres, twice Niagara's height, where the river goes over the edge of a lava flow into the canyon it has cut through the rotten, hydrothermally-altered rhyolite behind it. The green stripe down the face is where the water is deepest.

landmarks.name: Upper Falls of the Yellowstone
landmarks.info: Thirty-three metres, four hundred metres upstream of the Lower Falls, over the edge of a harder flow.

landmarks.name: Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone
landmarks.info: Thirty-two kilometres long, up to three hundred and sixty metres deep and twelve hundred wide. The yellow and pink of its walls is not the stone but what hot water has done to it - rhyolite rotted by the hot springs that once filled it - and the river has cut through it like cheese.

landmarks.name: Artist Point
landmarks.info: The view down the canyon to the Lower Falls that Thomas Moran painted in 1872. The painting is in the Capitol and helped get the park made.

landmarks.name: Tower Fall
landmarks.info: Tower Creek over a drop of forty metres, between columns of volcanic breccia that stand like the towers it is named for.

landmarks.name: Gibbon Falls
landmarks.info: Twenty-six metres down a stepped face that is a piece of the caldera's rim.

landmarks.name: Lewis Falls
landmarks.info: Where the Lewis River comes over the south rim of the caldera.

landmarks.name: Kepler Cascades
landmarks.info: The Firehole in a flight of steps, thirty metres in all.

landmarks.name: Firehole Falls
landmarks.info: Twelve metres, in the Firehole Canyon, in walls of rhyolite lava.

landmarks.name: Fairy Falls
landmarks.info: Sixty metres down a cliff of the Madison Plateau: a thin ribbon that goes to spray before it lands.

landmarks.name: Old Faithful Inn
landmarks.info: Built in the winter of 1903-04 of lodgepole and local rhyolite, with a lobby open seven storeys to the roof and a chimney of stone in the middle of it. The biggest log building in the world, and the house style of every national park lodge built after it.

landmarks.name: Lake Yellowstone Hotel
landmarks.info: The oldest hotel in the park, 1891, and the only one painted lemon yellow with a colonnade of Ionic columns on the lake - the colonial revival came in 1903, when the railway wanted something grander.

landmarks.name: Roosevelt Arch
landmarks.info: The North Entrance, at Gardiner. Theodore Roosevelt laid its cornerstone in 1903. 'For the benefit and enjoyment of the people', it says across the top, from the Act of 1872 that made this the first national park in the world.

landmarks.name: Mount Washburn Fire Lookout
landmarks.info: Three thousand one hundred and twenty-two metres up, on the rim of the older caldera, and on a clear day you can see the whole of the young one from it.

landmarks.name: Fort Yellowstone
landmarks.info: The army ran the park from 1886 until the Park Service existed, and built these for it: sandstone and brick, red roofs, a parade ground.

landmarks.name: Yellowstone Caldera
landmarks.info: Six hundred and thirty-one thousand years ago, the Lava Creek eruption emptied a magma chamber under here - a thousand cubic kilometres of ash, enough to bury the western half of the continent - and the roof fell in. This is the hole: seventy-odd kilometres by forty-five. Lava flows filled most of it since, and the rim is a scarp here and there rather than a wall. Under it, five to fifteen kilometres down, is the reservoir that is still partly molten. Press Caldera in the bar to see both.

landmarks.name: Sour Creek Dome
landmarks.info: One of the caldera's two resurgent domes: the floor pushed back up by magma underneath. It rises and falls by centimetres a year.

landmarks.name: Mallard Lake Dome
landmarks.info: The other resurgent dome, west of the lake, cut by faults across its top.

landmarks.name: Yellowstone Lake
landmarks.info: The largest high-altitude lake in North America: 350 km² at 2,357 m, frozen half the year. West Thumb is a caldera of its own inside the big one, and the floor of the lake has hot springs and explosion craters on it.

landmarks.name: Hayden Valley
landmarks.info: An old lake bed, silt and clay over the lava, where trees do not do well - so it is open grass, and the bison and the elk are here, and the traffic stops for them.

landmarks.name: Lamar Valley
landmarks.info: The Serengeti of North America, they call it: the big herds, and the wolves that were brought back in 1995.

landmarks.name: Eagle Peak
landmarks.info: The highest point in the park, 3,462 m, out in the Absarokas on the south-east boundary.

landmarks.name: Obsidian Cliff
landmarks.info: A lava flow that cooled to glass. People came from all over the continent for it for eleven thousand years, and Yellowstone obsidian turns up in burial mounds in Ohio.

landmarks.name: Norris Geyser Basin
landmarks.info: The hottest, oldest and most acid of the basins, where three faults cross; the ground changes year to year and the milky blue of the Porcelain Basin is silica in the water.
